prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Like nights we knelt on the dirt floor of a dugout, leaned our heads back, eyes twitching gone, and popped nitrous canisters into the communion shapes of our mouths, slipped inside where everything seemed to be falling snow, ice, the time split between chasing flies through a darkened park and sprawling in sycamore bark—how clean that abyss we drifted in, like dew, more like pollen, on our skins; and, beneath, a want for touch, a kiss, a return. Like nothing back then, to break an arm latching on to the bumper of an Impala, or settling back as the car took us as far as the salted bridge, before letting the ride go with a mitten caught behind the chrome waving from the other side of the river. Like this, you said, sliding a needle, watching dope plunge, the body's rush and tow until you felt something like an angel hovering above, but it was only pigeon feathers deviling the air. Those friends are gone: some dead, dying, locked up or jailed in themselves; and when I see some kids running in the heat of a taillight swirling behind them, I remember we wanted only to quiet our bodies, their unnatural hum, a vague pull inward, some thin furrows gliding over the snow.

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version that preserves the original imagery and meaning while refining its flow and cadence:

---

Like the nights we knelt upon the dirt floor of a dugout, tilted our heads back, our eyes twitching into nothingness, and pressed nitrous canisters to the communion-shape of our mouths, slipping inside where everything seemed to be falling snow, ice, the hours divided between chasing fireflies through a darkened park and sprawling against sycamore bark—how clean that abyss in which we drifted, like dew, or more like pollen, settling upon our skin; and, beneath it all, a longing for touch, for a kiss, for return.

Like nothing at all, back then, to break an arm while latching onto the bumper of an Impala, or to ease back as the car carried us as far as the salted bridge, before we let the ride go, a mitten still caught behind the chrome, waving from the far side of the river.

Like this, you said, sliding in the needle, watching the dope plunge—the body's rush and undertow—until you felt something like an angel hovering above, though it was only pigeon feathers deviling the air.

Those friends are gone now: some dead, some dying, some locked away, and some imprisoned within themselves. And when I see a few kids running in the heat of a taillight swirling behind them, I remember how we wanted only to quiet our bodies, their unnatural hum, that vague pull inward—those thin furrows gliding across the snow.

---

outputs.L2: On evenings when we would drop to the packed earth of a dugout, tip our heads backward, our eyes fluttering into blankness, and fit nitrous canisters against our lips shaped as if for communion, then dissolve into a place where all of it resembled snowfall, ice, that stretch of hours divided between racing after fireflies across a shadowed park and lying stretched out on sycamore bark—how pure that emptiness we floated through, settling like dew, or more truly like pollen, across our skin; and underneath it all, a craving to be touched, to be kissed, to come back. How easy it was in those days to snap a bone while gripping the fender of an Impala, or to lean into it as the car dragged us clear to the salt-covered bridge, then to release our hold with a mitten still snagged on the chrome, waving from across the water. Just like this, you told me, easing in a needle, watching the drug sink down, that surge and undertow through the body until you sensed something like an angel drifting overhead, though it was really nothing but pigeon feathers troubling the air. Those companions are all gone now: some dead, some dying, some behind bars or trapped within themselves; and whenever I catch sight of young kids darting through the swirl of a taillight's glow chasing after them, I recall how all we ever wanted was to still our bodies, to silence their strange buzzing, that faint tug turning us inward, those slender grooves sliding across the snow.
outputs.L3:
# Chasing Oblivion

I remember the dugout, and the way we would huddle there together, passing the small metal canisters between us. The nitrous hissed as it filled our lungs, and for a few precious seconds the world would dissolve into something soft and weightless. We were chasing that particular kind of oblivion—the dreamlike float where thought unraveled and the hard edges of everything went blurry and warm. It felt, in those moments, like slipping free of gravity itself, like drifting somewhere just beyond the reach of ordinary life.

But I understand now what we were really after, though none of us would have said it aloud back then. Beneath all our recklessness ran a current of something far more tender and desperate: we wanted to be touched. We wanted to be held. We were hungry for connection in a way that frightened us, and so we reached for canisters and pills instead of for each other. The drugs were a language we used because we didn't know how to speak the real one—the one about needing love, about wanting to matter to someone.

Our hunger took other forms too, ones that flirted more openly with death. In the depths of winter, when the roads turned to sheets of ice, we would crouch at the edge of the street and wait for a car to pass, then sprint out and grab hold of the bumper. We'd let ourselves be dragged along the frozen asphalt, laughing, our hearts slamming against our ribs. Any one of those nights could have ended with shattered bones or worse. We knew it, and somehow that knowledge was part of the appeal. The danger made us feel alive in a way that nothing else did.

I watched, too, as some of us went further. I remember the first time I saw heroin used—the ritual of it, the anticipation, the promise of some great transcendence waiting on the other side of the needle. But what I witnessed was not transcendence at all. The illusion collapsed almost as soon as it formed, leaving behind something small and gray and disappointing: a body slumped, a mind gone dull, a person diminished rather than elevated. Whatever they had been reaching for, it wasn't there. It never had been.

Most of them are gone now. Some are dead, others are dying slowly, and still others are locked away where the years pass without them. When I think back on all of it—the canisters, the icy roads, the needles—I see it for what it was. We weren't really chasing pleasure, or even oblivion. We were trying to quiet something restless that lived inside us, some ache we couldn't name and didn't know how to soothe. We threw ourselves against death again and again, hoping to silence it. But it was never the kind of hunger that danger or drugs could ever fill.
outputs.L4:
# Quieting the Body

We were the kids who couldn't sit still inside our own skin. There was a hum beneath everything—a low electric restlessness that wouldn't let us be. So we chased anything that might dial it down, might drown the noise, might finally let us feel quiet.

We sucked nitrous from cracked whippets in someone's basement, the world going soft and silver at the edges, our laughter arriving a half-second late like an echo from another room. The ceiling tilted. Our voices sounded borrowed. For those few spinning moments, the hum went silent, and silence felt like grace.

We caught rides we shouldn't have—clinging to the backs of moving cars, the asphalt blurring gray beneath our sneakers, wind tearing tears from the corners of our eyes. We told ourselves it was freedom. Really we were daring the world to keep us or discard us, laying our small lives across the open palm of chance just to feel the weight of being alive.

Some of us found the needle. I watched them draw the dope into the barrel, watched their faces smooth into something like peace, something I mistook for arrival. As if they'd finally reached the still place we were all chasing. As if the body could be talked down from its endless wanting.

But the body remembers what you do to it. It keeps the receipts.

Now when I count us, the math comes out all wrong. So many are dead—overdosed in bathrooms, wrapped around telephone poles, gone before they turned thirty. Others are locked away, serving out their sentences behind glass and wire. And some, the ones who technically survived, are trapped inside themselves—shut behind eyes that no longer light up, prisoners of the very stillness we once begged for.

That's the cruel joke of it. We wanted so badly to quiet our bodies, and the world obliged. It quieted them completely.

I'm still here. I don't fully understand why. Some mornings the old hum returns, that adolescent electricity, and I feel the ghosts of them beside me—still young, still reckless, still reaching for the silence that finally swallowed them whole. I carry them the way you carry a scar: not always visible, but always there, a map of everything we survived and everything we didn't.

We were only trying to feel still. We never knew stillness could cost so much.
outputs.L5:
# Grace on the Savanna

There is something mesmerizing about watching an impala move across the African plains. Unlike many other antelope, these creatures possess a lightness that seems almost impossible for a living thing. When startled, an impala can leap nearly ten feet into the air and cover distances of thirty feet in a single bound. Those spectacular jumps are not just for show—they serve as a survival mechanism, confusing predators and allowing the herd to scatter in unpredictable directions.

I remember the first time I saw them in the wild. Those graceful animals gathered near a watering hole at dawn, their reddish-brown coats catching the early light like polished copper. Like living statues, they stood alert, ears twitching at every sound. Then, without warning, one bolted, and the entire group followed in a breathtaking display of coordinated motion.

What makes the impala so successful is its adaptability. Like few other species, it thrives in both grasslands and woodlands, feeding on grass during the wet season and switching to leaves and shoots when conditions grow harsh. Those flexible eating habits allow herds to survive where pickier animals would perish.

The males, with their distinctive lyre-shaped horns, engage in fierce territorial battles during mating season. Those clashes can be dramatic, yet rarely fatal. Like most of nature's competitions, they follow rules older than memory itself, ensuring the strongest genes pass to the next generation.

To watch an impala is to witness pure elegance—a reminder that survival and beauty are not always at odds.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about a group of childhood friends and their descent into drug use, looking back from adulthood with grief and vivid sensory memory.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Summer Kept

We were seven once, or maybe six by the time it mattered, spilling off the same cracked porch into the blue hour when the streetlights buzzed awake and our mothers' voices carried thin across the yards. I still taste it—the metal of the garden hose, the way we drank standing up, sweat drying to salt on our necks, the whole neighborhood smelling of cut grass and someone's father grilling. We thought we would live forever because we had never once considered dying.

Then we were fifteen and the basement changed color. Danny's basement, wood paneling and a water heater that ticked like something counting down. The first pills came wrapped in a folded dollar bill, passed hand to hand the way we'd once passed baseball cards, and I remember thinking *this is nothing, this is just us,* the same as always, only warmer, only slower, the edges of everything gone soft as a bruise before it darkens.

You have to understand how good it felt. That's the part I can't make anyone believe—how the light through those small dirty windows turned gold and holy, how we laughed until our stomachs hurt, how loved I felt, how held. Grief is dishonest if it pretends the poison never tasted sweet.

Marcus went first. They found him in a car with the engine running and the radio still on, playing the songs we grew up on. Then it was Katie, quiet Katie who used to braid the long grass into crowns, gone in a bathroom that wasn't even hers. Then Danny, whose basement it was, whose laugh could fill a room, folded up on a mattress in a city none of us had ever visited, alone in a way we swore we'd never let each other be.

I am forty now. My daughter has the same gap in her teeth that Katie had, and when she laughs the whole kitchen fills with someone twenty-five years dead. I keep the porch light on. I don't know why. Maybe so the boys I loved can find their way back through the blue hour, dripping garden water, still seven, still certain, still standing in the last summer before we learned what our own hands were for.

We were children. We were only ever children, holding out our palms, taking whatever was offered, believing every gift was mercy.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a single-paragraph prose poem that begins with "Like nights" and uses a series of "Like" comparisons to explore memory, addiction, and lost friends.
counterfactuals.output: Like nights that arrive before the sun has finished dying, before you've decided whether to let them; like the burn of a first drink at fourteen, holy and terrible, the way it made the room soften and forgive you; like Danny's laugh in the passenger seat, gone now, a sound I can almost hold if I stop breathing; like the needle's small mercy, which was never mercy but a landlord collecting rent on every good thing; like the phone number I still know by heart though the man who answered it is ash and rumor; like standing in a kitchen at 3 a.m. wanting something I could no longer name, only its shape, only the hole where it used to fit; like the friends who became photographs, who became stories, who became the silence I keep in my mouth like a stone; like the year I mistook for a life; like remembering, which is its own slow substance, its own vein; like the way I say their names now—Danny, Rae, the ones the winters took—not to bring them back but to prove I was there, that I loved them badly and completely, the only way I knew, like nights.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a lyrical, elegiac piece in the style of a confessional poet remembering reckless youth—huffing nitrous, hitching rides on car bumpers, shooting heroin—and how those friends are now dead, dying, or in prison.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Living Owe

We were seventeen and made of nothing
that could break—or so we told ourselves,
sucking silver from the whippet's throat,
the world gone soft and singing at the edges,
laughter dopplering away like sirens
we were always just outside of.

Remember Danny on the back of Kessler's Chevy,
knuckles white against the chrome,
his sneakers sparking off the blacktop,
how we screamed for him to hold on—
how we screamed because we loved
the terror more than we loved him?

There was a summer made entirely of thresholds:
the needle's small mouth, the spoon's black kiss,
the way the heroin came in like a tide
that never once suggested it might leave us
face-down in the aftermath.

*

Now I count them on a hand that shakes.

Kessler in the ground since '09,
the crash we all somehow survived
except him, saving it up.
Danny doing fifteen upstate,
his letters thinning to a line.
Marie, who taught me how to tie off,
still walking but already gone,
a ghost that hasn't gotten the news.

*

And I am here, which is its own accusation—
awake at forty in a quiet house,
paying my taxes, watering the fern,
alive for no good reason I can name
except that death, that summer, looked away
and blessed me with its inattention.

What do I do with all this borrowed time?
I write their names. I say them into the dark
the way we used to call each other's houses,
letting it ring and ring,
believing someone, somewhere,
was still young enough to answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dense, image-rich prose poem about escaping the body's "unnatural hum" through drugs and dangerous games, ending with the speaker seeing kids today and remembering.
counterfactuals.output:
The Unnatural Hum

There was a frequency in me before I knew the word for frequency—a wire strung too tight behind the sternum, a refrigerator drone that never cut to silence, the body idling at a pitch only I could hear. So I went looking for the off-switch in all the wrong cathedrals.

First the pills, chalk-white communion wafers pocketed from medicine cabinets like small moons, and how the hum would soften then, would blur into a warm and cottoned nothing, the world gone underwater and me finally floating instead of thrashing. Then the games—oh, the games. We took turns fainting behind the gymnasium, hands pressed to throats until the sky went granular and starred, until we dropped like felled saplings and woke to grass-print on our cheeks and the exquisite gift of a mind wiped clean of its terrible radio. We raced trains, not to die but to feel the platform of ourselves shudder, to replace the inner noise with something so loud and iron and immediate that there was no room left for the hum.

I remember the reservoir at midnight, the black water swallowing us to the collarbone, the dare passing between us like a shared cigarette. I remember the highway median at two a.m., headlights strobing our laughter into stop-motion. I remember believing danger was a kind of medicine, that to court the edge was to finally quiet the machine, that if I could just get close enough to ending I might learn how to begin.

We were not sad, exactly. We were loud boys trying to outshout an inner weather. We were tuning forks looking for a hand to still us.

Now I am older than that reservoir, older than those trains. I stand at the corner with my coffee cooling and I watch them pass—the kids, hoods up, earbuds in, that particular electric flinch in the shoulders, that look of listening to something no one else can hear. And I know. God help me, I know exactly the pitch of it, the wire behind the sternum, the search for the off-switch, the beautiful stupid hunger to be, for one clean second, quiet.

I want to tell them: it fades. It doesn't leave, but it fades. You learn to live beside the hum like a house beside a highway, until the sound becomes a kind of silence, until you almost—almost—miss it when it's gone.

They wouldn't hear me over the noise. I didn't either.

So I just watch them go, and I remember, and I let them.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem exploring themes of numbness, longing for touch, and mortality, using imagery of snow, pollen, pigeons, and a car crossing a salted bridge.
counterfactuals.output:
**Salted Bridge**

I have gone numb the way snow goes numb,
forgetting it was ever water,
forgetting the shape of falling
into anyone's open hand.

Somewhere the pollen is loosening,
that yellow insistence, that ache
to touch and be received—
but I am glassed in, I am January,

and the pigeons on the wire
hunch their gray theologies,
saying nothing of spring,
saying *stay, stay, the cold is honest.*

I drive the salted bridge at dusk.
The salt is here to keep us
from the slick beneath,
the way the body scatters caution

against its own dark water.
I want a hand on the back of my neck.
I want to be a field in April,
undefended, humming with bees.

But the bridge is long,
the river underneath moves black and patient,
learning my name the way rivers do—
slowly, then all at once.

The pigeons lift. The pollen drifts
toward a season I may not reach.
And still I press the pedal,
still I cross, still salt

dissolves beneath me into nothing,
doing its brief and stubborn work:
holding the surface,
holding me a little longer, up.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
